did_you_know.text: The words matzevah and maskit stone probably refer to ritual or decorated stones. The prohibition distinguishes using stone as decoration from bowing before it.

The verse places two kinds of holiness side by side: the holiness of time in Shabbat and the holiness of place in the sanctuary. Holiness is therefore part of both the calendar and the physical world.
In ancient Israel, where summers are usually dry, the timing of rain was extremely important for farming. Rain “in its season” mattered almost as much as the amount of rain.

The verse describes an almost unbroken agricultural cycle: threshing lasts until the grape harvest, and the grape harvest until sowing. It portrays abundance in which the new harvest arrives before the old one is finished.
In Biblical Hebrew, revavah means ten thousand. The numbers are not just military arithmetic; they also emphasize the strength of a united community.
In the ancient world, grain and food were stored for long periods, so “old” did not necessarily mean spoiled. Here, the old harvest is removed because there is more new produce than can be stored.
The word komemiyyut is probably related to standing upright. In contrast to a slave bent under a yoke, the people are pictured walking upright and free.
Shechefet and kaddachat are names of illnesses, but their exact modern diagnoses cannot be identified with certainty. Ancient translations also understood them in different ways.
“Skies like iron” and “earth like bronze” are metal images for drought: the sky gives no rain and the ground produces nothing. The verse does not mean that the sky and earth literally become metal.
Returning the bread “by weight” suggests rationing during famine. Ten women using one oven also reflects a time when basic resources have become scarce.

The term chammanim is probably connected with sun worship or objects dedicated to it, though its exact meaning is uncertain. Here it appears alongside high places and idols in a critique of foreign worship.
The rest that the land “makes up” is connected with the sabbatical year, when farmland is meant to lie fallow. Exile is portrayed as a time when the land receives the rests it had missed.
The image of a rustling leaf describes fear so intense that a tiny sound seems dangerous. It is a psychological description of anxiety, not merely a description of military defeat.

The ancestors are named here as Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham, rather than in the more usual order. The list emphasizes that all the generations belong to the same covenant, along with the land mentioned in the verse.

Even after the harsh description of exile, the verse says that the covenant is not canceled. This is an important idea: punishment is not presented as the complete destruction of the relationship between God and Israel.
